351.title: The one-letter meter
351.hook: ajai alai abhai abai: unconquerable, indestructible, fearless, unchanging (Jaap, ek achhari)
351.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the ek achhari stanzas near the end of Jaap Sahib very quickly, and many know the line ajai, alai, abhai, abai by heart.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breaker of the cruel, and your line, break cruelty, adorn earth. Did you refuse one small cruelty? Today, Jaap's most compressed meter, where the words are almost all one sound. Day three hundred fifty-one.
screen: `BREAKER OF THE CRUEL — BREAK CRUELTY, ADORN EARTH.`

segments.voice: Try this. Say ah. Just the sound, mouth open, nothing else. It's the sound at the doctor's office, the sound of relief when you sit down after a long day, the sound of surprise. In Gurmukhi, it has its own letter, airha, near the very start of the alphabet. Now put that sound at the front of almost every word in a stanza, and build the whole meter on it. Jaap Sahib has one. Today: the one-letter meter.
screen: `SAY AH.` → `A SOUND WITH ITS OWN LETTER.` → `A STANZA BUILT ON IT.`

segments.voice: The meter is called ek achhari. Ek is one, achhar is a letter. The one-letter meter. Sikh teachers explain the name in more than one way, but you can hear the plainest reason straight away: almost every word in these stanzas begins with the same letter, the a that means without. Here's the first line: ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Four words, four doors closing on four old fears. Ajai. Jai is victory, being conquered, so ajai is unconquerable. Nobody defeats the One. Alai. Lai is dissolving, being destroyed, so alai is indestructible. Nothing wipes the One away. Abhai. Bhai is fear, so abhai is fearless. Abai. Bai is age, wearing down, so abai is ageless, unchanging. Unconquerable, indestructible, fearless, unchanging. Listen to what's underneath that list. Defeat, destruction, fear, decay. Call them four shadows over a human life: losing, being wiped out, being afraid, getting old. And each one is answered with a single short a. It's almost the opposite of everything Jaap has said so far, the long names, the Persian titles, the doubled words. Here the praise gets very small, and very fast. Some reciters fly through these lines so quickly they sound like rain on a roof. The one-letter meter sounds like the hymn running out of room for anything but the essentials. And Jaap keeps coming back to one of these four in particular. Tomorrow, the one in the middle: abhai.
screen: `EK ACHHARI: THE ONE-LETTER METER.` · `AJAI: UNCONQUERABLE. ALAI: INDESTRUCTIBLE.` · `ABHAI: FEARLESS. ABAI: UNCHANGING.` · `FOUR SHADOWS, FOUR SHORT ANSWERS.` · then, large: `AJAI, ALAI, ABHAI, ABAI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the four words slowly. Ajai. Breathe. Alai. Breathe. Abhai. Breathe. Abai. Breathe. Let each one land. Then say them a little faster, the way they're recited, ajai, alai, abhai, abai, and feel the rhythm. Then stop, and sit with the open sound of a, the one at the front of every word. The bell holds the time.
The one-letter meter. Ek achhari, where nearly every word begins with a: ajai, alai, abhai, abai, unconquerable, indestructible, fearless, unchanging.
screen: `THE ONE-LETTER METER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Today, when you feel beaten, worn down or afraid, say the four words once under your breath. Day three hundred fifty-one.

352.title: Fearless, changeless
352.hook: the Jaap keeps returning to fearlessness, a quality at the heart of the Khalsa ideal
352.howItsDone: Sikhs say nirbhau, without fear, every day in the Mool Mantar and abhai many times in Jaap Sahib, and fearlessness without hatred is central to the Khalsa ideal.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one-letter meter, and your line, ajai, alai, abhai, abai. Did you say them once when the day pushed back? Today, the third of those four words, the one Jaap keeps coming back to. Day three hundred fifty-two.
screen: `THE ONE-LETTER METER — AJAI, ALAI, ABHAI, ABAI.`

segments.voice: Fear has a body. A tight chest before the phone call. Cold hands before the exam results open. A stomach that drops when the boss says, got a minute? Plenty of people carry a few fears around like stones in a pocket: money, health, being left, being found out. We get so used to the weight that we forget it's there, until something makes us reach in and touch one. Jaap Sahib, recited every morning, keeps saying one word against that weight. Today: fearless, changeless.
screen: `FEAR HAS A BODY.` → `STONES IN A POCKET.` → `A WORD SAID AGAINST THE WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: The word is abhai. Bhai is fear; a is without. Fearless. Count how often it comes back in Jaap. It's in the one-letter meter, ajai, alai, abhai, abai. It returns again and again in other stanzas, alongside its partners: unconquerable, unchanging, unborn. Of all the qualities Jaap praises, fearlessness is one it simply won't let go of. Sikhs met the idea long before Jaap. The Mool Mantar, at the very start of the Guru Granth Sahib, calls the One nirbhau, without fear, and nirvair, without hatred, side by side. Guru Nanak's opening and the Tenth Guru's praise agree. Then comes the turn that matters for daily life. Sikhs don't praise fearlessness only as something God has. They hope to grow toward it. The ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Tenth Guru's father, wrote that the wise person is the one who frightens no one, and fears no one. Both halves. Not a bully, and not a coward. And Sikhs remember him living it: tradition tells of him going to Delhi and to his execution rather than abandon the freedom of others to practice their faith. Fearlessness sits at the heart of the Khalsa ideal his son founded: a people meant to stand up without fear and without hate, and never to put fear into the innocent. That's the logic of the carry, as Sikh teachers often put it: people grow a little like what they praise every morning. Saying abhai doesn't make fear vanish. The hope is that fear stops being the one deciding.
screen: `ABHAI: WITHOUT FEAR.` · `NIRBHAU, NIRVAIR: THE MOOL MANTAR.` · `FRIGHTEN NO ONE, FEAR NO ONE.` · `GROWING LIKE WHAT YOU PRAISE.` · then, large: `FEARLESS LIKE HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one fear and breathe. Reach into the pocket and pick up one stone. Name it, silently and plainly: I'm afraid of this. Notice where it sits in your body: chest, stomach, shoulders, jaw. Breathe into that place, slowly, without trying to make the fear leave. Just let it be held. Then, if you like, say abhai on the out-breath, a few times. Not to argue with the fear. Just to remind it who else is here. The bell holds the time.
Abhai. Without fear: the quality Jaap keeps returning to, echoing nirbhau in the Mool Mantar.
screen: `ABHAI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: fearless like him. Today, do one small thing you've been putting off out of fear, and do it without frightening anyone else. Day three hundred fifty-two.

353.title: Present in every land
353.hook: the Jaap salutes the One who dwells in every country and every garb
353.howItsDone: Sikhs around the world recite Jaap Sahib in the same words every morning, and gurdwaras far from Punjab close their gatherings with the Ardas's prayer for sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, abhai, without fear, and your line, fearless like him. Did you do one thing you'd been putting off? Today, Jaap looks out across the whole map. Day three hundred fifty-three.
screen: `ABHAI — FEARLESS LIKE HIM.`

segments.voice: Open a map of gurdwaras on your phone and zoom out. Southall, in west London. Surrey, near Vancouver. Yuba City in California. Nairobi, Kuala Lumpur, Melbourne, Singapore, a small town in northern Italy. Little markers scattered across the map. Behind each one, someone who left Punjab, carried the Guru's words in a suitcase, and found that the morning prayers still worked in a new time zone. Long before any of that, the Tenth Guru wrote praise that fits every one of those places. Today: present in every land.
screen: `A MAP OF GURDWARAS, ZOOMED OUT.` → `MARKERS SCATTERED ACROSS THE MAP.` → `THE PRAYERS WORK IN A NEW TIME ZONE.`

segments.voice: Throughout Jaap, the One is saluted as dwelling everywhere: in every country, in every kind of dress, in water and on land. One short chachari line says it in four words: jale hain, thale hain. You are in the water. You are on the land. And near its very end, Jaap calls the One chatar chakkar vartee, present in all four directions, every point of the compass. Think about what every garb means in the Guru's world. Clothing told everyone who you were: a Hindu holy man's saffron, a Muslim scholar's robe, a soldier's armor, a farmer's rough cotton, a queen's silk. Jaap salutes the One in all of them, and Sikhs read it plainly: no land is holier by birth, and no costume is closer to the Divine. Sikhs have a long habit of living that line. Tradition remembers Guru Nanak walking for years, east toward Assam, south toward Sri Lanka, north into the mountains, west as far as Mecca and Baghdad, sitting with people of every faith he met. And today Sikhs pray the Ardas in Toronto and Birmingham and Bangkok with the same closing words you met at the end of year one: sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Not the good of Punjab. The good of all. In that reading, every land is somewhere to pray, and every stranger in every garb is someone the One is already with.
screen: `EVERY COUNTRY, EVERY GARB.` · `JALE HAIN, THALE HAIN: WATER AND LAND.` · `CHATAR CHAKKAR VARTEE: ALL DIRECTIONS.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA: THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `IN EVERY LAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a faraway place kindly. Choose somewhere you've never been, or somewhere in the news, or the place your family came from. Picture it as clearly as you can: the streets, the weather, the people waking up or going to sleep there right now. Breathe in, and picture them. Breathe out, and wish them well, plainly: may they be safe, may they be fed. If you pray, you can hold them in the words sarbat da bhala. The bell holds the time.
Present in every land. Jaap's salutation to the One in every country and every garb, in water and on land, in all four directions.
screen: `PRESENT IN EVERY LAND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: in every land. Today, when you hear a place name in the news, any place at all, wish the people there well for one breath. Day three hundred fifty-three.

screen: `DAY 353 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BEYOND THE FEAR OF DEATH.`

354.title: Beyond the fear of death
354.hook: praising the One who ends all things loosens the fear of our own ending
354.howItsDone: At Sikh funerals, mourners recite Kirtan Sohila and the Ardas, and the Sikh code of conduct asks them to recite and remember rather than wail, understanding death as the soul's return to the One.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, present in every land, and your line, in every land. Did you wish a faraway place well? Today, a gentle day about the hardest subject there is. Day three hundred fifty-four.
screen: `PRESENT IN EVERY LAND — IN EVERY LAND.`

segments.voice: There are plenty of ways of not thinking about it. We change the subject. We say passed away instead of died. We get through a funeral and go straight back to email. And then, at three in the morning, or in a hospital corridor, or on the anniversary of someone's going, the thought comes anyway: one day, me too. Traditions answer that three a.m. thought in different ways. Jaap Sahib answers it in a surprising way, not by talking about death less, but by naming the One who holds it. Today: beyond the fear of death.
screen: `WE CHANGE THE SUBJECT.` → `THE THREE A.M. THOUGHT.` → `JAAP NAMES WHO HOLDS IT.`

segments.voice: All through Jaap, the One is praised as the ender of all things. Sarab kaal. And in one bhujang prayat line, namo kaal kaale: salutation to the death of death, the One who is the end even of endings. It might seem a grim thing to say every morning. But follow the logic. If death were a stranger, an enemy who could sneak up from outside, then fear would make sense. Jaap says it isn't. Death isn't a rival power. It's in the One's hand, the same hand Jaap has called merciful, the house of compassion, the sustainer of all. In Jaap's picture, an ending isn't decided by a stranger. It's held by the One saluted every dawn. Sikh scripture goes further, and some of its voices meet death almost gladly. Bhagat Kabir, whose words are in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that the death the whole world fears fills his mind with joy, because only through dying comes perfect, supreme bliss. Sikh teaching speaks of the soul returning to its source, like a drop to the ocean. That shapes how Sikhs mourn. At a Sikh funeral, people recite Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime prayer, and the Ardas. The Sikh code of conduct asks mourners not to wail or beat their chests, but to recite gurbani and remember Waheguru. Grief is real, and tears are human; no one is asked to pretend. But the hymns are recited anyway, because, as Sikhs see it, the one who has gone has gone home. Death is in his hand. In Jaap's picture, so is everyone death touches.
screen: `NAMO KAAL KAALE: DEATH OF DEATH.` · `NOT A STRANGER: IN THE ONE'S HAND.` · `KABIR: THE DEATH THE WORLD FEARS.` · `AT A FUNERAL, SOHILA AND ARDAS.` · then, large: `DEATH IS IN HIS HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit one minute with calm. Sit comfortably and let your breath slow down. Notice that every out-breath is a small letting go, and every in-breath comes back without you asking. If someone you love has died, you can hold them gently in mind; if that's too heavy today, simply rest. Let your hands lie open in your lap, as if resting in larger hands. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Beyond the fear of death. In Jaap, death is not a stranger but in the hand of the One praised as merciful, so fear can loosen.

355.title: Keeping the pace
355.hook: the meters quicken like drums; many recite Jaap briskly, as marching music for the spirit
355.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Jaap Sahib briskly from memory each morning, letting its quickening meters carry them, and in a gurdwara a whole sangat may recite it together at speed.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, beyond the fear of death, and your line, death is in his hand. That was a quiet day. Today, the opposite: Jaap at full speed. Day three hundred fifty-five.
screen: `BEYOND THE FEAR OF DEATH — DEATH IS IN HIS HAND.`

segments.voice: Boom. Boom. Boom-boom-boom. The marching band is still two streets away, and already your shoulders have gone back. Your step falls into time without permission. The kids on the curb start stomping, and a grandmother on a bench taps her cane. Nobody decided to keep the beat; the beat picked them up and carried them. That's what a steady rhythm does to a body. Tired legs keep going, and a wandering mind stays in line. Jaap Sahib knows that. Today: keeping the pace.
screen: `DRUMS BEFORE YOU SEE THE BAND.` → `YOUR STEP FALLS INTO TIME.` → `THE BEAT CARRIES YOU.`

segments.voice: Over the last three weeks you've heard Jaap change its walk again and again. The snake's long glide of bhujang prayat. The quick two-word steps of chachari. The tiny lines of harbolmana. The one-letter meter, ek achhari, where the words shrink to almost nothing. Listen to them in order, and you notice: as the hymn goes on, many of the lines get shorter, and the pace gets quicker, like a drummer speeding up toward the end of a song. That's why many Sikhs recite Jaap briskly, not slowly and solemnly. Ask around and you'll hear it described as marching music for the spirit. It has what Indian poetics calls bir ras, the heroic mood, the feeling of standing tall and moving forward. It fits the Guru who wrote it, who was a poet and a leader of soldiers at once. But the speed isn't only about courage. It's also about attention. When you recite slowly, the mind has time to wander off to lunch. At pace, there's no room. Each line arrives right behind the last, and you have to stay with it. The praise carries you, the way the drums carry a tired marcher. It's the same idea as day three hundred thirty-two, praise at pace, now heard from the inside.
screen: `GLIDE, STEPS, TINY LINES, ONE LETTER.` · `THE PACE QUICKENS LIKE A DRUMMER.` · `BIR RAS: THE HEROIC MOOD.` · `AT PACE, NO ROOM TO WANDER.` · then, large: `MARCH IN PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite ten lines briskly, ten you already know. Tap your knee for the beat. Namastvam akaale. Namastvam kripaale. Namastvam aroope. Namastvam anoope. Aroop hain. Anoop hain. Ajoo hain. Abhoo hain. Karunaalay hain. Khal khanddan hain. Once slowly to find them, then once more at pace, without stopping. Feel your back straighten. Then sit still and let the beat fade. The bell holds the time.
Keeping the pace. Jaap's meters quicken like drums, and many Sikhs recite it briskly, as marching music for the spirit.

356.title: The last stanza
356.hook: sadaa sachidaanand: ever truth, consciousness and bliss, breaker of enemies, dwelling in all (Jaap 199)
356.howItsDone: Sikhs end their morning recitation of Jaap Sahib with these closing stanzas, often reciting them from memory, before moving on to the Tav Prasad Savaiye.

screen: `DAY THREE-HUNDRED-FIFTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, keeping the pace, and your line, march in praise. Did a walk fall into a beat? Today, after all its stanzas, Jaap comes home. Day three hundred fifty-six.
screen: `KEEPING THE PACE — MARCH IN PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Some music ends by coming home. The orchestra has wandered through storms and dances and quiet passages, and at the end, the themes from the opening come back, gathered up, all the instruments together, one last chord. The music says: we've arrived. Jaap Sahib ends in a similar way. It doesn't introduce a stranger in its last lines. It gathers what it has said, and the languages it has said it in. Today: the last stanza.
screen: `THE THEMES COME BACK AT THE END.` → `ALL THE INSTRUMENTS TOGETHER.` → `ONE LAST CHORD.`

segments.voice: Near the very end, back in the gliding bhujang prayat where the salutations began, comes this line: sadaa sachidaanand, satr pranaasee, kareemul kuninda, samastul nivaasee. Take it slowly. Sadaa: always, ever. Sachidaanand is three Sanskrit words fused: sat, truth or being; chit, consciousness; aanand, bliss. Ever truth, consciousness and bliss. Then satr pranaasee: the destroyer of enemies, the protector you met in the armed One and the breaker of the cruel. Then the language changes in mid-line. Kareemul kuninda: Kareem is Arabic, the Generous; kuninda is Persian, the Maker. The generous Maker. And samastul nivaasee: the One who dwells in all, present in every land. Listen to what just happened. In one line, Sanskrit and Arabic and Persian sit side by side, the same mix the whole hymn has used. Bliss, protection, generosity, presence everywhere: themes from all the past three weeks, gathered in one breath. That's the final chord. And the stanza that seals the hymn ends with these words: sadaa ang sange, ever with you, by your side, close as your own limbs. After stanza upon stanza of names too vast to picture, timeless, formless, king of kings, sun of suns, Jaap's last word is not far away at all. It's right here. Ever true, ever bliss, and ever beside you.
screen: `SADAA SACHIDAANAND: EVER TRUTH, BLISS.` · `KAREEMUL KUNINDA: THE GENEROUS MAKER.` · `THREE LANGUAGES IN ONE LINE.` · `SADAA ANG SANGE: EVER BY YOUR SIDE.` · then, large: `EVER TRUE, EVER BLISS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the last line aloud. Slowly, in the snake's rhythm: sadaa sachidaanand, satr pranaasee, kareemul kuninda, samastul nivaasee. Say it twice. Then say the sealing words once, gently: sadaa ang sange. Ever by your side. Put a hand on your arm or over your heart as you say it, and feel how close that is. Then sit with the closeness. The bell holds the time.
The last stanza. Jaap's final chord: ever truth, consciousness and bliss, the generous Maker dwelling in all, and ever by your side.

357.title: Jaap and the amrit bowl
357.hook: Jaap is one of the five banis recited over the iron bowl as amrit is prepared
357.howItsDone: At Amrit Sanchar, the Panj Pyare stir water and sugar in an iron bowl with a khanda while reciting Japji, Jaap, Tav Prasad Savaiye, Chaupai and Anand Sahib; the initiates drink the amrit from the same bowl.

segments.voice: A grandmother making soup. She doesn't just stir. She talks while she stirs: to the pot, to the kids in the doorway, sometimes under her breath to God. People who grew up in kitchens like that will swear the soup tasted different from anyone else's. Maybe it was the recipe. Maybe it was everything that got stirred in with it. There's a Sikh ceremony where that idea is taken with complete seriousness: words are stirred into water for a long time, and Sikhs say the water is never the same again. Today: Jaap and the amrit bowl.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER STIRS AND TALKS.` → `THE SOUP TASTED DIFFERENT.` → `WORDS STIRRED INTO WATER.`

segments.voice: When a Sikh chooses to take amrit and join the Khalsa, the ceremony is called Amrit Sanchar. Five initiated Sikhs, the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, kneel around an iron bowl, a bata, filled with clean water. Into the water go patashe, small sugar sweets. Then the water is stirred with a khanda, a double-edged sword, while the Panj Pyare recite five banis, one after another. The first is Japji, Guru Nanak's. The second is Jaap Sahib. Then the Tav Prasad Savaiye, then Chaupai, then Anand Sahib. All of it, every stanza, is recited over the water as it's stirred. Think about what that means for Jaap. The salutations you've been learning, akaal, kripaal, aroop, ajooni, abhai, are recited into the water the new Khalsa drinks. The amrit is sprinkled on their eyes and hair, and they drink from the same bowl, whatever caste or family they came from. Tradition traces the ceremony to Vaisakhi in 1699, when the Tenth Guru first prepared amrit at Anandpur. A much-loved part of the story says the Guru's wife brought sugar sweets to the bowl, so that the iron and the steel would be joined by sweetness. Sources differ on the details, but Sikhs often say the point is clear: courage and kindness, stirred together. And this is where the week ends: the one-letter meter, abhai, fearlessness, the One in every land, death held in the One's hand, keeping the pace, the last stanza. And today, all of it, stirred in.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stir a glass of water, reciting. This isn't amrit, and isn't meant to copy the ceremony. It's just a way to feel what words stirred into water might mean. Fill a glass. Stir it slowly with a spoon, round and round, and as you stir, say a line you know: namastvam akaale, namastvam kripaale. Then stop, set the spoon down, and drink the water slowly, noticing it go in. The bell holds the time.
Jaap and the amrit bowl. Jaap is the second of the five banis recited over the iron bowl as amrit is stirred for the Khalsa.
